summary: A Southeast Asian archipelagic country made up of more than seventeen thousand islands, with the world's fourth-largest population and the largest Muslim population of any country; it declared independence from the Netherlands in 1945.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: From the 13th century Muslim merchants from Gujarat, Arabia and Persia came to the archipelago along the maritime trade routes, and Samudera Pasai in northern Sumatra became one of the earliest Islamic kingdoms (its sultan's gravestone dates from 1297). In the 15th century the Sultanate of Malacca arose, and the Sultanate of Demak in Java rose after the decline of the Hindu kingdom of Majapahit, with the "Nine Saints" (Wali Songo) spreading the faith in ways that blended with local culture. Islam spread mainly through trade and peaceful means, making Indonesia the country with the largest Muslim population in the world; Muhammadiyah (founded 1912) and Nahdlatul Ulama (1926), established in the early 20th century, are still the largest Muslim organizations.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: After the Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602, Calvinism was introduced to eastern islands such as Ambon; in the 19th century Ludwig Nommensen of the German Rhenish Missionary Society succeeded in preaching among the Batak of Sumatra, and places such as Minahasa in North Sulawesi, Papua and Toraja also became Christian areas through missionary work. After 1965 the government required citizens to register one official religion, so many followers of traditional beliefs registered as Christians, raising the proportion of Protestants.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 16th century the Portuguese evangelized in the Maluku Islands and the Lesser Sunda Islands, and Saint Francis Xavier went to Maluku in 1546–1547. In the early Dutch period Catholicism was suppressed, and missionary work resumed only after the 19th century. Today Catholics are concentrated on the island of Flores in East Nusa Tenggara province, in western Timor, and in parts of Papua.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: From the 5th century kingdoms influenced by Indian culture appeared in Java and Sumatra, the Prambanan temple was built in the 9th century, and the Hindu Majapahit Kingdom, founded in 1293, was one of the most powerful dynasties in the history of the archipelago. After the rise of Islamic kingdoms in the 15th–16th centuries, some Majapahit nobles and priests withdrew to Bali, making Bali the only province in Indonesia today that is predominantly Hindu, with about ninety percent of residents following Balinese Hinduism.

ranking.name: Buddhism and Confucianism
ranking.description: The Srivijaya Kingdom of the 7th century was a center of Buddhist learning, where the Tang monk Yijing stayed to study; in the 9th century the Sailendra dynasty built Borobudur. After Islamization Buddhism almost disappeared from the archipelago, and today Buddhists and Confucians are mainly ethnic Chinese Indonesians. Confucianism was not recognized in the Suharto period and Chinese culture was suppressed, until it was lifted by President Wahid in 2000, after which it was restored, and Lunar New Year has also been a public holiday since 2003.

religion.background: The Indonesian archipelago originally worshipped ancestral spirits and nature spirits, and from the early centuries AD, under Indian influence, Buddhist and Hindu kingdoms such as Srivijaya, Sailendra and Majapahit appeared. After the 13th century Islam came through maritime trade and in the 15th–17th centuries gradually became the faith of most regions, blending with local culture. From the 16th century Portuguese and Dutch colonization brought Catholicism and Protestantism, which took root mainly on the eastern islands. At independence in 1945 the "Five Principles" (Pancasila) were made the basis of the state, believing in God without founding an Islamic state, and currently six religions are officially recognized.

ranking.name: Javanese
ranking.description: Javanese is the language of the Javanese of central and eastern Java, and the Javanese are Indonesia's largest ethnic group, so it has the most native speakers. The Old Javanese (Kawi) inscriptions and literature from the 9th century were deeply influenced by Sanskrit; in the 17th century the court culture of the Mataram dynasty developed a strict system of honorific speech levels, requiring different registers according to the status of the person addressed. Although Indonesian is the national language, Javanese remains the home language of tens of millions.

ranking.name: Indonesian (as a mother tongue)
ranking.description: Indonesian is based on Malay, which since the Srivijaya era in the 7th century had been the trade lingua franca of the archipelago. In the "Youth Pledge" of October 28, 1928, nationalist youth proclaimed "Indonesian" as the unifying language; the ban on Dutch during the Japanese occupation of 1942–1945 further raised the status of Indonesian, and the 1945 constitution made it the national language. Because it is not the language of the largest ethnic group, it is more acceptable to all groups, and the number of people with it as a mother tongue is growing quickly in big cities such as Jakarta and in interethnic marriage families.

ranking.name: Sundanese
ranking.description: Sundanese is the language of the Sundanese of West Java, and the Sundanese are Indonesia's second-largest ethnic group. The historical Sunda Kingdom (Pajajaran) was destroyed by Islamic kingdoms in the 16th century, but Sundanese language and culture continued, and likewise developed a system of honorifics. The provincial capital Bandung is the center of Sundanese culture, and Sundanese is still widely used in homes and local media in West Java.

language.history: Indonesia has more than seven hundred languages, most belonging to the Austronesian family, while the Papua region has a large number of Papuan languages. The ancient kingdoms wrote inscriptions in Sanskrit, Old Malay and Old Javanese, and after Islamization the Arabic script was adopted to write Malay (Jawi). In the Dutch colonial period Malay was used as the administrative lingua franca, and a Latin-alphabet spelling was drawn up in the early 20th century. The "Youth Pledge" of 1928 established Indonesian as the language of national unity, after independence it spread across the country through education and the media, and in 1972 the spelling was unified with Malaysia. Today most Indonesians use both a regional language and Indonesian.

ranking.name: Nasi goreng (Indonesian fried rice)
ranking.description: White rice is stir-fried with sweet soy sauce (kecap manis), shallots, garlic, chili and shrimp paste, and served with a fried egg, prawn crackers and pickled cucumber.
ranking.history: The technique of fried rice is generally thought to come from Chinese immigrants, who brought the habit of frying leftover rice to the archipelago, and Indonesians added sweet soy sauce, shrimp paste and chili to form a local flavor, originally a breakfast made from the previous day's leftover rice. In the Dutch colonial period it was one of the dishes of the "rijsttafel" and traveled with the colonizers to the Netherlands. In 2018 the Indonesian tourism ministry listed it as one of five national dishes, and when U.S. President Obama visited Indonesia in 2010 he also mentioned missing the fried rice he ate in his childhood.

ranking.name: Beef rendang
ranking.description: Pieces of beef are slowly simmered for hours in coconut milk with spices such as lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and chili, until the liquid has reduced and the meat is dark brown.
ranking.history: Rendang originates with the Minangkabau of West Sumatra and is an essential dish at their weddings, festivals and traditional ceremonies. Cooking it for a long time until dry lets it keep for weeks at room temperature, and Minangkabau men have a tradition of leaving home to seek their fortune (merantau), often taking rendang with them on the road; the dish also spread across the country and Malaysia with their "Padang restaurants". In 2011 it ranked first among the "world's most delicious foods" in a CNN readers' poll and became internationally known.

ranking.name: Satay
ranking.description: Marinated small pieces of chicken, beef or mutton are skewered on bamboo sticks and charcoal-grilled, drizzled with peanut sauce or sweet soy sauce, and eaten with rice cakes (lontong) and shallots.
ranking.history: Satay is generally thought to have taken shape in Java in the early 19th century, possibly influenced by the Indian and Middle Eastern kebabs brought by Muslim traders; the peanut sauce poured over it uses peanuts that the Portuguese and Spanish introduced from the Americas after the 16th century. Different versions developed in different places, such as Madura satay and Padang satay. It is one of the most common street snacks in Indonesia, and is also often made in large quantities at festivals such as Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

ranking.name: Gado-gado
ranking.description: Blanched vegetables, tofu, tempeh, boiled egg and rice cakes are tossed with a thick peanut sauce and sprinkled with fried shallots and prawn crackers; the flavor is sweet and slightly spicy.
ranking.history: The name means "mixed" and is generally thought to come from the Betawi people of Jakarta. The tempeh it uses is a fermented soybean food invented by the Javanese hundreds of years ago, the tofu came from Chinese immigrants, and the peanut sauce comes from a crop of the Americas, fully showing the diverse blending of Indonesian food. Because it is mainly vegetables, it is one of Indonesia's most popular vegetarian dishes, often appearing at street stalls and family lunches, and is also one of the five national dishes.

ranking.name: Soto
ranking.description: A yellow soup boiled from chicken or beef with spices such as turmeric, lemongrass and galangal, eaten with rice vermicelli, bean sprouts, boiled egg and rice.
ranking.history: The name is generally thought to derive from the Hokkien name of a soup brought by Chinese immigrants in the 19th century, which then absorbed local spices in different places, forming dozens of regional versions, such as Jakarta's coconut-milk beef soup (soto Betawi), Lamongan chicken soup of East Java, and Makassar's "coto". It is a common choice for Indonesians at breakfast and lunch, served from roadside stalls to restaurants, and is also listed as one of the five national dishes.
